**Algorithmic Economics** is a structured learning and research programme at the intersection of economics and computer science. It studies economic institutions as computational systems and develops the technical toolkit required to analyse, simulate, design, and evaluate them.

The programme is organised into two complementary parts.

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
## [Part I — Economics × Computer Science](part1/index.qmd)

Markets, mechanisms, networks, strategic interaction, social choice, platforms, and digital institutions.

Part I asks:

> **What economic and institutional problems become computational problems?**

[Enter Part I →](part1/index.qmd)
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
## [Part II — Computational and AI Research Toolkit](part2/index.qmd)

Research computing, machine learning, causal ML, deep learning, optimisation, reinforcement learning, multi-agent learning, and foundation models.

Part II asks:

> **What computational, statistical, and AI tools are needed to study and design these systems?**

[Enter Part II →](part2/index.qmd)
:::
::::

## Learning philosophy

The programme does not treat economic theory, computation, data, and artificial intelligence as separate subjects. Wherever possible, learning follows the sequence

\[
\text{economic question}
\rightarrow
\text{formal model}
\rightarrow
\text{algorithm}
\rightarrow
\text{implementation}
\rightarrow
\text{data or simulation}
\rightarrow
\text{replication}
\rightarrow
\text{research extension}.
\]

The emphasis is on **active, reproducible, research-oriented learning**. Learners are expected not only to understand models, but also to implement algorithms, work with real or simulated data, reproduce results, evaluate institutions, and formulate extensions.

## Programme objectives

By completing the programme, a learner should be able to:

- move fluently between economic and computational formulations of a problem;
- reason about incentives, equilibrium, welfare, information, and strategic behaviour;
- understand and discuss algorithms, computational complexity, optimisation, and network structures;
- implement economic and computational models in reproducible research workflows;
- use modern statistical learning, causal machine learning, deep learning, and sequential-decision methods;
- analyse real markets, platforms, allocation systems, and digital institutions;
- reproduce and critically evaluate theoretical, computational, and empirical research;
- collaborate effectively across economics and computer science;
- identify research questions at the frontier of algorithmic economics.

## What the programme produces

The intended final outcome is not simply completion of a sequence of courses. Learners should leave with a **research portfolio** containing implementations, data laboratories, replications, case studies, and one or more substantial research projects.

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}

Data labs, replication exercises, module projects, and capstones connect theory to implementation and evidence.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## How should I use the programme?

The programme is designed to be flexible.

**Follow the full sequence** if you want a systematic route through economics and computer science.

**Enter selectively** if you already have strong preparation in particular areas.

**Use Additional Resources** when you need to strengthen prerequisites or explore a topic beyond the formal programme.

**Use the projects as checkpoints.** A topic is not considered mastered merely because its lectures or readings have been completed.
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## How are resources selected?

Resources are ranked by their usefulness for the learning objective rather than by geography or institution. Where several excellent resources exist, they are combined rather than substituted. The programme deliberately includes material from the UK, Europe, North America, Latin America, Asia, and elsewhere, in English and Spanish where high-quality material is available.
:::

## Start

**New to the economics–computer science interface?** Begin with [Part I](part1/index.qmd).

**Already comfortable with game theory, mechanisms, markets, and algorithms?** You may begin with [Part II](part2/index.qmd) and use Part I selectively.
